data.title: Furuncle and carbuncle — viva
data.summary: Bacterial infections · 13 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Furuncle and carbuncle** (Bacterial infections)_

**Q1. Define furuncle and carbuncle.**
- Furuncle (boil): acute deep necrotising infection of a single hair follicle and its surrounding tissue, usually by S. aureus, forming a tender red nodule that suppurates and discharges a core
- Carbuncle: a cluster of interconnecting furuncles extending into subcutaneous fat, with multiple openings (sieve-like) — usually back of neck, back, thighs

**Q2. What are the predisposing factors? (frequently asked)**
- Nasal/perineal carriage of S. aureus (most important for recurrence)
- Diabetes mellitus, obesity, malnutrition, iron deficiency anaemia
- Immune defects: HIV, chronic granulomatous disease, hyper-IgE (Job's) syndrome, neutrophil dysfunction, chemotherapy, steroids
- Friction, sweating, poor hygiene, occlusive clothing, crowding (hostels, prisons, sports teams)
- Atopic dermatitis; PVL-producing community MRSA

**Q3. Where do furuncles not occur and why?**
- Palms and soles — no hair follicles

**Q4. What is the danger area of the face?**
- Triangle from the corners of the mouth to the bridge of the nose — venous drainage via angular and ophthalmic veins to the cavernous sinus; squeezing a boil here can cause cavernous sinus thrombosis

**Q5. What is Panton–Valentine leukocidin (PVL)?**
- Pore-forming S. aureus toxin that destroys neutrophils; linked to recurrent boils, abscesses in families/close contacts, and necrotising pneumonia
- Suspect when boils recur in several family members

**Q6. Differential diagnosis of a furuncle?**
- Hidradenitis suppurativa (flexural, recurrent, sinus tracts, double comedones)
- Inflamed epidermal/pilar cyst, acne conglobata nodule
- Myiasis (furuncular), deep fungal infection, kerion (scalp)
- Anthrax (black eschar, painless) for carbuncle
- Erythema nodosum (no fluctuation)

**Q7. Complications?**
- Cellulitis, lymphangitis, bacteraemia, septicaemia; osteomyelitis, endocarditis, septic arthritis
- Cavernous sinus thrombosis (face); scarring; glomerulonephritis is not a feature of staphylococcal infection
- Carbuncle in diabetics: extensive necrosis, ketoacidosis

**Q8. Management of a furuncle.**
- Moist warm compresses to bring to a point
- Incision and drainage once fluctuant — the single most important step for a large lesion; send pus for culture
- Systemic antibiotics if >1 cm with cellulitis, face, multiple lesions, systemic features, immunosuppression: cloxacillin/cephalexin; MRSA — doxycycline, clindamycin, cotrimoxazole, linezolid
- Do not squeeze lesions on the face

**Q9. Management of a carbuncle.**
- Admit if large, diabetic or toxic; control blood sugar
- Parenteral antibiotics (cloxacillin/cefazolin, vancomycin for MRSA)
- Surgical drainage / cruciate incision and debridement of necrotic tissue; dressings; skin graft for large defects

**Q10. Approach to recurrent furunculosis.**
- Exclude diabetes, anaemia, HIV; check neutrophil function/IgE if childhood onset
- Culture swabs of nose, axilla, groin (patient and family)
- Decolonisation: mupirocin to nares twice daily for 5 days (repeat monthly), chlorhexidine 4% body wash or dilute bleach bath twice weekly, treat whole family
- Long-term low-dose clindamycin 150 mg daily for 3 months has evidence; rifampicin 600 mg with cloxacillin/doxycycline for 10 days for carriers
- Hygiene: separate towels, hot wash of bed linen, nails short

**Q11. Histopathology of furuncle?**
- Perifollicular neutrophilic abscess with necrosis of the follicle extending into dermis and subcutis; Gram-positive cocci

**Q12. What is a stye (hordeolum)?**
- Furuncle of an eyelash follicle / gland of Zeis; internal hordeolum = Meibomian gland infection

**Q13. What is botryomycosis (asked as a short note)?**
- Chronic granulomatous bacterial infection (usually S. aureus, also Pseudomonas) producing nodules, sinuses and grains — mimics mycetoma
- Grains show Gram-positive cocci with Splendore–Hoeppli material; treat with prolonged culture-guided antibiotics ± excision

## Quick spotter facts
- Danger triangle of face — cavernous sinus thrombosis
- Recurrent boils in a family — think PVL-positive S. aureus

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (ch. Pyodermas); Rook's Textbook of Dermatology for cross-check. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
